title: How the 3.7L Mustang Starting System Works
introduction:
The Engine Start/Stop button makes a request; the starter motor does the muscle work. Between them, the car checks key authorization and pedal inputs, passes information between controllers, and switches the starter circuit. I think of it as a relay race with an actual relay near the finish.

I read the drawings from the button inside the FCIM toward the BCM, then the PCM, starter relay and starter motor. The pedal and transmission inputs join that path from above and below. Use the labeled drawing to understand the relationships and the numbered drawing with its separate item table to identify components. The message charts explain what information travels between modules.

This is an operating overview, not a wiring test or replacement procedure. Some module connections and anti-theft descriptions conflict within the supplied references; those differences remain identified below rather than becoming a guessed circuit map.

requirements.category: Key recognition before a start attempt

items.name: Use a programmed passive key inside the vehicle
items.detail: The BCM must recognize a valid programmed passive key before the ignition can leave OFF. A key being physically inside the car does not guarantee detection at the cabin’s outer edges.

items.name: Respond to No Key Detected
items.detail: If the key is in a door map pocket, above a sun visor or at a far corner of the luggage compartment, move it away from that area and try turning the ignition on again. Some mobile-phone or laptop chargers can interfere with recognition; move the key away from a nearby charger and retry. See the [PATS operating description](#/document/G1694659) for the separate backup-starting method and its required key orientation.

edits.text: Here is the path from a start request to an engine that cranks, followed by the jobs of the components involved.
edits.why: Separating the request, authorization and switching stages helps explain why pressing the button does not directly power the starter motor.

I follow the arrows from the switch inside the FCIM to the BCM, across HS1-CAN to the PCM, and onward through the starter relay to the starter motor. The drawing also shows brake and clutch inputs reaching both controllers, while the automatic-transmission input enters the PCM. These are functional relationships, not connector locations or probing instructions.
A network message carries information between controllers. It is a different part of the starting story from the circuit that supplies the starter.

edits.text: Messages Received by the Powertrain Control Module (PCM)
edits.why: Read each row across from the broadcast message to its originating module and purpose. This identifies what the receiving controller is being told; it does not show a connector pin or an electrical test value.

edits.text: Messages Received by the Body Control Module (BCM)
edits.why: This table has a source conflict: it names an RFA identification exchange and says an incorrect response disables PATS. The complete linked PATS description instead identifies a PCM challenge to the BCM: a correct reply permits starting, while an incorrect reply prevents it. Do not read the ambiguous table as permission to start after a failed identity check. I use the explicit authorization description below and retain this disagreement visibly.

edits.text: The passive anti-theft system (PATS) can prevent engine cranking when key or controller authorization fails. The IPC displays the corresponding message if a PATS concern disables the engine. See [Passive Anti-Theft System (PATS) - System Operation and Component Description](#/document/G1694659) for the complete authorization account. Reference section: 419-01B.
edits.why: The starting overview names an invalid PCM ID; the linked PATS account is more explicit about the exchange: the key sends identification to the RTM, which passes it to the BCM over LIN, and the PCM challenges the BCM for a valid reply. A correct reply releases starting inhibition; an incorrect reply prevents starting. I follow that explicit sequence here, while flagging the older identity wording rather than pretending the sources agree. Think of the key check as admission at the door and the controller exchange as checking the guest list again inside.

edits.text: The BCM sets the ignition mode. The push-button switch has direct inputs to the BCM and PCM, as described in this overview’s switch section and in [Steering Wheel and Column Electrical Components - System Operation and Component Description](#/document/G1693266). Reference section: 211-05.
edits.why: The earlier operating paragraph also names an RFA module, which conflicts with its own switch description. The primary starting drawing shows the BCM-to-PCM path, and the matching ignition drawing explicitly shows the direct switch connections. I use those documented connections for this explanation; the conflicting RFA account is not a verified extra module or route.

edits.text: An additional paragraph in the starting source describes a backup arrangement between an RFA module and BCM, carrying a failed switch circuit’s request over MS-CAN. That particular backup route conflicts with the direct BCM/PCM account and remains unconfirmed.
edits.why: Redundancy means another path can carry a request after a failure, but that general idea does not prove which wires or controllers this vehicle uses. I retain the disputed backup description as a source limitation, not a route to trace or a circuit to bypass. Use the applicable verified wiring information for electrical diagnosis.

edits.text: A start request combines the push-button input with the brake-pedal input for an automatic transmission or the fully depressed clutch input for a manual transmission. When the PCM recognizes the correct inputs, it supplies voltage and ground to the starter relay coil. The energized coil closes the relay contacts, which supply voltage to the starter solenoid so the starter motor can crank the engine. The PCM disengages the starter motor when an engine Revolutions Per Minute (RPM) threshold is reached, the set cranking time is exceeded, or the ignition switch - push button start is pressed to request engine shutdown.
edits.why: The relay coil is the control side; its contacts switch the supply to the solenoid. That distinction explains how a small button can request cranking without carrying starter current. The PCM also controls when cranking ends, so the button does not need to remain held to keep the starter engaged. No numerical cranking limit or engine-speed threshold is specified here. The original operating paragraph includes RFA among the recipients; that participant is part of the same unresolved conflict above, not an additional confirmed step in this explanation.

edits.text: On the automatic-transmission vehicles covered here, remote start lets the operator start the engine with the Passive Key from up to 30 meters (98 feet) away. The engine then runs for 10 minutes, and the operator can extend that run time. Use the Owners Guide for the operating details and extension instructions. For information about enabling remote start, refer to [Handles, Locks, Latches and Entry Systems - System Operation and Component Description](#/document/G1695897) (501-14 Handles, Locks, Latches and Entry Systems, Description and Operation) and the Owners Literature.
edits.why: Keep the automatic-transmission qualifier attached to this feature. The range and run time describe its operation; enabling it and extending the run time require the referenced instructions, which are not reproduced here.

edits.text: With the operating sequence in mind, here is what the button and controllers contribute.
edits.why: This connects the component descriptions to the request-to-cranking sequence.

edits.text: The ignition switch - push button start, labeled Engine Start/Stop, is a momentary-contact switch hardwired to the BCM and PCM. It requests the OFF, ON or START ignition modes. The switch is part of the front controls interface module (FCIM) and cannot be serviced separately. For its operation and ignition-mode details, refer to [Steering Wheel and Column Electrical Components - System Operation and Component Description](#/document/G1693266) (211-05 Steering Wheel and Column Electrical Components, Description and Operation).
edits.why: Momentary contacts act while the button is pressed rather than mechanically latching an ignition state. The linked description identifies normally open contact sets that provide a ground input to the BCM and a voltage input to the BCM and PCM. Its drawing supports these direct connections, which conflict with the earlier RFA-based account. The service restriction also means the button is not described as an independently replaceable part.

edits.text: For the BCM’s broader functions, refer to [Module Controlled Functions - System Operation and Component Description](#/document/G1692963) (419-10 Multifunction Electronic Modules, Description and Operation).
edits.why: For this overview, I keep the BCM’s role tied to authorization, ignition mode and the information passed toward the powertrain controller. The referral remains necessary for its broader functions; this article does not teach module replacement or programming.

edits.text: The PCM supplies power and ground to the starter relay to initiate engine cranking.
edits.why: This is the controller’s switching command to the relay coil. The relay contacts then supply the starter solenoid, completing the handoff from an electronic request to mechanical cranking.

readerOutcome: Understand the source-supported request, authorization and relay sequence while recognizing the explicitly unconfirmed legacy RFA/MS-CAN backup account. This overview does not authorize wiring diagnosis, bypass, module programming or complete starting procedures.
teachingNotes: Every requested primary text block is rewritten under its original block ID. Headings remain concise single-line titles, and the original tables and illustrations remain separate.
The diagram explanation distinguishes functional signal paths from physical wiring, connector access and test instructions.
Primary numerical values, units, section identifiers, service restrictions and referrals remain in their original blocks. No cranking threshold or time limit has been invented.

The complete supporting text, tables, raw text and all attached illustrations were considered. Supporting material supplies relevant key-recognition preparation and the authorization explanation without expanding this overview into programming, replacement or steering-lock service.
Backup starting remains an explicit referral to the PATS instructions and orientation illustration. Remote-start enabling and extension instructions likewise remain referrals.
The RFA architecture and anti-theft identity conflicts are exposed for focused technical correction rather than silently resolved.

Conflicting module and PATS table claims remain visibly disclosed, with confirmed direct inputs tied to matching primary component text and supplied ignition/PATS descriptions. The RFA backup route remains explicitly unconfirmed, not silently replaced or omitted.

sourceReconciliation.scope: Independently assess a bounded operating overview: retain conflicting original evidence and explicitly disclose unresolved RFA backup route; do not treat an incorrect identity response as start authorization. Complete primary and supports/figures already included. More recent revision alone is not proof. Evaluate primary component text/diagram versus explicit linked architecture. Reject if marked uncertainty still makes this informational coverage misleading.
